column3: The archival expansion interprets winning Qin's alliance; the instructor's name changes. Conquering Qin is a different relation.
The recommendation, its failure and death all matter; adding Li as a surname or repeating words damages the answer.
Movement from Yue to Qi survives in the shorter modern wording, but it loses flight. The reverse destination is wrong.
Qi attacks Zhao. The reciprocal event has the wrong participants.
Chu as an army is an added restriction. The doubled Zheng demonym weakens one rendition.
The appointment is of Liao Li after Liu Bei becomes king; collecting revenue is unrelated.
The threat is to douse it. The contextual gloss gives this reading, but the supplied line alone does not establish the name or fire scenario.
Bao joins Chu in attacking Han. The repeated time phrases are awkward.
The governed realm is compared with something turned in the palm. Compassion needs to survive in modern language.
The appointment at a distance and both offices matter. The plainer partial version leaves the recipient and distant appointment unclear.
The requested direction is Qi against Qin. A conditional about not wanting an attack misstates the question.
The troops entering Qi survive in several fragments; counting cooking stoves differs from feeding a hundred thousand.
The malformed preposition leaves the relationship recoverable. The reversed invasion fails.
An assault on a city is more specific than attacking the state; annihilating the city and adding a duke are extra claims.
The site is Hanzhong. A defeat taking place in Chu itself changes the location.
The question asks whether the achievements of two ministers can recur under a new government.
Assaulting Yan city is the event; merely going there loses the attack.
Fighting in Hanzhong differs from defeating the territory or fighting in Qin.
The action is encirclement, not merely an unspecified joint attack. Reversal invalidates it.
Bao initially attacks Chu together with Han. Defeating Chu is stronger than striking it.
Zhao is the attacker; a terse but grammatical modern verb suffices.
Selecting a younger son sets a bad political example. Several answers turn appointment into a campaign.
The distich has difficult wording. The interpretation about succession and radiance is plausible but uncertain.
The order is to inspect customs and identify illegality across the prefectures.
Chu campaigns against Qin. An unexplained joint action is additional.
Relatives and friends express amazement when he returns.
The Yan commander follows Zhao to relieve Chu. Following without the rescue loses the event.
The assignment is to lead Qi troops into Wei and make a hundred thousand stoves.
The visitor arrives in the capital and is asked about attaining longevity in the palace.
The object is securing Han with the king of Qin. The archival rendering changes the instructor's name.
The appeal asks why the listener does not use Qin to attack Qi. A negative conditional changes the appeal.
The commander follows Chu to relieve Zhao; just following Chu leaves the beneficiary missing.
The speaker or account has only this to say.
The siege of Cai has Chu as aggressor.
The exact flight is from Qi to Yue; escaping from the army misstates the source of flight.
Qin attacks Chu. Joint attack adds an unexpressed ally.
